entry.title: How to unlock the Feedback Resonator in Subnautica 2
entry.summary:
The Feedback Resonator is an advanced modification for the Sonic Resonator that you'll need to reach the endgame in Subnautica 2. It allows us to solve a puzzle that activates the fourth Angel Comb.
But first, we will need to find the blueprint fragments.
Table of contents Feedback Resonator blueprint locations in Subnautica 2 How to craft the Feedback Resonator in Subnautica 2
Feedback Resonator blueprint locations in Subnautica 2
Before you reach the blueprint locations, you'll need to upgrade your Tadpole with the Depth Module Mk. 1, or it will take damage, as the blueprint is located at almost 600m depth.
With that out of the way, head east from your lifepod. You'll first reach the Alien Ruins, where the Research Outpost is. From there, head a few metres straight, and you'll reach the Power Center. Dive down, and you'll find the Angel Comb.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Go straight from the Angel Comb, and you'll find a room with a pool full of toxic green liquid. Go a few metres forward, and look to your left. You'll find the first fragment by a rock.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Next, return to your Tadpole and swim 50m upwards. Then head straight past the pool, and you'll find a pink light glowing in the dark.
Screenshot by Destructoid
There's a platform at the base of this light, with the second fragment on it. Scan the second fragment, and you'll unlock the Feedback Resonator blueprint.
How to craft the Feedback Resonator in Subnautica 2
Screenshot by Destructoid
To get the Feedback Resonator, you'll need the Modification Station.
While the Feedback Resonator will require a Sonic Resonator, it will be added as a separate device in your inventory.

entry.title: How to unlock Modification Station in Subnautica 2
entry.summary:
The Modification Station allows us to improve our tools in Subnautica 2 vastly, allowing us to explore the late-game content in the current early access build. We can use the station to improve our Tadpole submarine and upgrade tools like the Sonic Resonator.
The first task is to unlock the blueprint.
Table of contents Modification Station blueprint location in Subnautica 2 How to use Modification Station in Subnautica 2
Modification Station blueprint location in Subnautica 2
To unlock the Modification Station, you'll have to scan just one blueprint. You can find the blueprints at multiple locations, but I have stuck to the easiest one in this guide. To reach this location, you won't need any advanced tools. However, I recommend using the Wakemaker to cover the distance quickly.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Head out about 1300m from the lifepod to the east, and you'll find the Alien Ruins. You'll find the Research Outpost at a depth of about 140m (to the left of the large alien tower). If you've dived too deep, use the space bar to ascend.
Head in through the entrance, and you'll find the Engine Efficiency upgrade on your right. Next, go in through the main tunnel and turn right. You'll find the Modification Station; complete the scan, and the blueprint will be available.
Screenshot by Destructoid
How to use Modification Station in Subnautica 2
Screenshot by Destructoid
Once you're back home, you can now place the Modification Station using your Habitat Builder (assuming you have the resources). Open the station, and you'll find a list of all the available modifications, all of which have different resource costs.
The modification will be applied automatically once you craft it using the Modification Station.

entry.title: How to unlock the Tadpole in Subnautica 2
entry.summary:
The Tadpole is an amazing vehicle we can use for our deep-sea exploration in Subnautica 2. It allows us to explore the true depths that's not possible otherwise. But first, you'll need to unlock the blueprint fragments.
Tadpole blueprint fragment locations in Subnautica 2
To unlock the Tadpole, you'll need to find three blueprint fragments. These fragments have different locations. However, I have chosen the best spots where you're relatively safe from any predators or environmental hazards. You'll need a larger oxygen tank, since that's the only concern.
Screenshot by Destructoid
To find the location, we will have to head towards 190 degrees on the compass. The location is approximately 145m away from the lifepod, at an approximate depth of 90m. Your first indication will be the coral reef in the image above, which has debris to its left.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Go past the reef, and dive deep. You'll come across a crash site with the first part. Scan the fragment, and return to the surface to refill your oxygen.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Next, dive at the same spot, and turn right. You'll want to follow the path that goes right until it ends. Turn right, and you'll find a hatch with a room inside. Head inside, and you'll be able to refill your oxygen. More importantly, the second tadpole blueprint fragment is on a shelf against the wall.
Screenshot by Destructoid
Head outside, and go straight. You'll find a massive coral reef, and the final blueprint will be at its foot.
Screenshot by Destructoid
A note of caution: this coral is located quite deep, and you'll run out of your oxygen more quickly. Hence, have backup plans so that you can reach the surface immediately. You should also save immediately after finding the third and final fragment.
The post How to unlock the Tadpole in Subnautica 2 appeared first on Destructoid.

entry.title: "We tried something different": Looking back on SiN Episodes: Emergence, the Valve-backed shooter that tried and failed to kick off an age of episodic gaming
entry.summary: On May 10, 2006, Ritual Entertainment released SiN Episodes: Emergence, the first of nine episodes set in the sci-fi megalopolis of Freeport City. Backed by Valve and launched on Steam just a month before Valve's own Half-Life 2: Episode 1, the game felt like it was the start of something new. Ritual even had Gabe Newell singing their significance, saying in Emergence's launch day press release that "With the release of SiN Episodes: Emergence Ritual is leading the industry's long overdue migration to producing episodic content." Valve famously released just two Half-Life episodes before stalling. Ritual only ever managed one. But, as I learned when talking to some of its creators, SiN Episodes: Emergence is much more than a hiccup in the history of gaming, it was a title torn between the old publishing traditions of the 90s and newly emerging technologies of the 00s. entry.summary:
This week the former Zachtronics folk of Coincidence released U.V.S. Nirmana, a new "Zach-like" puzzler that has fairly spaghettified my synapses, despite being billed as "medium-difficulty". It puts you in charge of a monastic spacecraft embarked on a pilgrimage through the galaxy, steeped in references to Dharmic religions. During your voyages, you'll help other civilisations with their philosophical dilemmas using a cosmic reactor that functions like a music sequencer. You'll join up pipes and components to resolve relationships between terms like "form", "amen" and "svaha", doing your best to minimise "flux".
Playing the opening few puzzles, I felt a mixture of excitement and guilt. Excitement, because while I barely understand what's going on, I love the ritual obtuseness of, say, trying to distil "light" and "sound" into "thought" by means of valves and relays. And guilt, because it turns out original Zachtronics founder Zach Barth told me about this game two years ago, and I forgot. entry.title: Amberspire review - a strategy game dedicated to the dicey ecopoetics of urban sprawl
entry.summary:
The key thing to know about Amberspire is that it isn't a city-builder in the SimCity sense, but a turn-based boardgame puzzler in which you don't so much 'build' a city as you do manage a tumult of unpredictable, city-flavoured agencies. Created by Lunar Division, developers of The Banished Vault, it takes place on the surface of a moon-sized mausoleum - a vast Venetian graveworld whose fractured isometric crust reveals level after level of archways and catacombs, sinking beyond sight.
The all-pervading presence of the crypt reminds me of London's old church cemeteries, crushed like dandelions between mishappen skyscrapers, refusing to be written out of the tale. It also immediately undercuts your primary objective of building a city populous and advanced enough to win recognition from other planets. However high your towers rise, your city is just another layer of debris and pollution applied to a strangely fruitful necropolis. This isn't a lesson in humility. It's an invitation to enjoy city-building as the act of dancing with a deathly ecology.

Priyanshu Kumar will port the iBASS engine to ScummVM. This engine was written by Revolution Software in order to release Beneath a Steel Sky with enhanced controls and features on iOS, and the upgrades to the engine will be incorporated into ScummVM to benefit all platforms. Ramyak Sharma will be dedicating his summer to focus on the DIRECTOR engine, bringing more features and compatibility to the Macromedia Director preservation effort, and enhancing its Visual Debugger. Please give them all a warm welcome and feel free to visit our Discord server to discuss their projects. The community bonding period starts today, and the coding period will follow, starting on the 25th of May. You can expect regular updates on their respective blogs on Planet. With the four GSoC students on board, the team is already in a Summer of Coding state of mind — we hope you’re joining us in the countdown!
